items.item: Hive-style partitioning stores data in directories with partitioning column values encoded in the path itself
a data source implements this interface specifically to push filters down and reduce how much data a scan reads

at.deep: DSv2 partition-stats filtering, the sourced-only half

items.item: RangePartitioning's own 'sampled' mechanism (named in the syllabus clause as 'sampled range partitioner') samples the data first to estimate range boundaries before the real shuffle runs — a separate sampling job this topic's own plan-text measurement doesn't independently isolate, since the rangepartitioning tag alone confirms the partitioner used, not the sampling step that chose its boundaries.

at.out: the sampling step behind range partitioning's own boundary selection named only; not independently measured

items.item: DSv2's own partition-stats filtering (named in the syllabus clause alongside static Hive-style pruning) is a separate mechanism from directory-based pruning: a DSv2-compatible source can report per-partition statistics a query can filter against at plan time, without that source necessarily using Hive-style directories at all — this topic's own examples.py measures the directory-based case specifically, disclosing the DSv2 statistics path as sourced-only via its own interface.

at.out: DSv2 partition-stats filtering named via SupportsPushDownFilters.java; not independently measured against a real DSv2 source

items.item: HashPartitioning's own partition-id formula (a modulo of a Murmur3 hash of the partitioning expressions) is deterministic and version-pinned specifically because stateful streaming operators depend on the same row always landing in the same partition across restarts — a correctness requirement named in the source's own scaladoc, beyond the batch-query partitioning this topic measures.

at.out: the Murmur3-hash partition-id formula and its streaming-correctness requirement named only; this topic measures batch partitioning behaviour

items.item: A third family, dynamic partition pruning (DPP), uses a runtime filter result from one side of a join to prune the other side's partitions at execution time, not at plan time — a different mechanism from this topic's own static, plan-time pruning, covered as its own later topic in this chapter.

at.out: dynamic partition pruning named only; this topic measures static, plan-time pruning specifically

items.item: ShuffleExchangeExec's own ENSURE_REQUIREMENTS tag (visible in a real plan alongside REPARTITION_BY_NUM for an explicit repartition call) marks a shuffle the planner added itself to satisfy an operator's required distribution — the exact mechanism this topic's own same-key/different-key window comparison exercises, distinguishing a planner-added shuffle from a user-requested one.

at.step: Reveal: one shuffle, shared across both

items.item: Static partition pruning requires the filter predicate to reference the partitioning column directly and be resolvable at plan time (a literal or a foldable expression) — a filter whose value is only known at runtime (such as a subquery result) cannot prune statically at all, which is precisely the gap dynamic partition pruning exists to close.

at.out: the static-pruning predicate requirement named only; the runtime case is dynamic partition pruning, a separate later topic

items.item: A hash-partitioned join between two tables, each already partitioned by the join key with matching partition counts, exercises the exact same exchange-elimination mechanism this topic measures via window steps — a join's own ClusteredDistribution requirement is satisfied the same way a window's PartitionBy requirement is, just on a different physical operator.

at.out: exchange elimination on a join's own ClusteredDistribution requirement named only; this topic measures the mechanism via window operators specifically

items.item: Spark's own ReusedExchange node (distinct from the plain Exchange-elimination this topic measures) appears when two genuinely identical subplans, not merely two compatible distribution requirements, get deduplicated into one physical execution — a related but separate optimisation from the requirement-satisfaction case this topic's own examples.py isolates.

at.out: ReusedExchange named only as a related, separate mechanism; this topic's own measurement isolates requirement-based elimination, not subplan deduplication

items.item: AQE's own runtime coalescePartitions feature, disabled for this topic's whole session, can merge small post-shuffle partitions together after execution begins — a dynamic, cost-based adjustment layered on top of the static Exchange count this topic measures from the up-front plan, and would otherwise obscure the exact 1-vs-2 contrast the window comparison relies on.

at.out: AQE's own coalescePartitions runtime adjustment named only; this topic disables AQE specifically to keep the up-front plan-time Exchange count legible

items.item: Bucket pruning, the storage-partitioned-join mechanism this chapter covers next, differs from this topic's own directory-based static pruning in that it skips whole files within a directory by a hash of the bucketing column rather than skipping whole directories by an equality predicate on a Hive-style partition column — a related but distinct pruning granularity this topic does not measure.

at.out: bucket pruning named only as the next topic's own, finer-grained mechanism; this topic measures directory-level static pruning specifically
